ety.text: The verb is from Middle English crien (13th century), from Old French crier, from Vulgar Latin *crītāre, generally thought to derive from Classical Latin quirītāre (Proto-West Germanic *krītan has also been suggested as a source). The noun corresponds to Middle English cry, crie, from Old French cri, a deverbal of crier.

senses.d: To shed tears; to weep, especially in anger or sadness.
ex: That sad movie always makes me cry.
- Emerl: “There’s nothing worse than making a girl cry!” That’s what Sonic said...

senses.d: To utter loudly; to call out; to declare publicly.
ex: All, all, cry shame against ye, yet I'll speak.
[T]he Man put his fingers in his Ears, and ran on crying, Life, Life, Eternal Life: [...]

senses.d: To shout, scream, yell.
ex: And about the ninth hour, Jesus cried with a loud voice.

senses.d: To forcefully attract attention or proclaim one’s presence.
ex:
My secrets cry aloud.
I have no need for tongue.

senses.d: To utter inarticulate sounds, as animals do.
ex: the young ravens which cry
In a cowslip's bell I lie / There I couch when owls do cry.

senses.d: To cause to do something, or bring to some state, by crying or weeping.
ex: Tonight I’ll cry myself to sleep.

senses.d: To make oral and public proclamation of; to notify or advertise by outcry, especially things lost or found, goods to be sold, auctioned, etc.
ex: to cry goods
Love is lost, and thus she cries him.

senses.d: Hence, to publish the banns of, as for marriage.
ex: I should not be surprised if they were cried in church next Sabbath.

senses.d: A shedding of tears; the act of crying.
ex: After we broke up, I retreated to my room for a good cry.

senses.d: A shout or scream.
ex: I heard a cry from afar.

senses.d: Words shouted or screamed.
ex: a battle cry

senses.d: A clamour or outcry.
A group of hounds.
ex: A cry more tunable / Was never hollaed to, nor cheered with horn.
sometimes I have known such a cry of hounds at uncoupling to take the game at counter

senses.d: A pack or company of people.
ex: Would not this […] get me a fellowship in a cry of players?

senses.d: A typical sound made by the species in question.
ex: "Woof" is the cry of a dog, while "neigh" is the cry of a horse.

senses.d: A desperate or urgent request.
Common report; gossip.
ex: The cry goes that you shall marry her.

pt:chorar.gl: to cry; to weep (to shed tears from the eyes)

ety.text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese chorar, from Latin plōrāre (“to lament”). Compare Galician chorar and Spanish llorar.

Inherited from Old French hurler, from Vulgar Latin ūrulāre, from Latin ululāre, from a reduplicated Proto-Indo-European imitative root. Doublet of hululer. The h- might be due to influence by Frankish *hūilōn, from Proto-Germanic *hūwilōną; compare English howl.
Inherited from Middle French crier, from Old French cri(d)er, from Vulgar Latin *crītāre.

pt:berrar.gl: to yell loudly or angrily, to scream

ety.text: Either imitative or inherited from Vulgar Latin *verrāre, from verrēs (“boar”). Compare Spanish berrear and Romanian zbiera.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese braadar, from Vulgar Latin *balatrāre (“to shout, to shriek”), probably related to Latin balatrō (“charlatan”), probably from balō (“to baa”). Cognate with Galician bradar, Spanish baladrar, Catalan baladrejar.

Deverbal from chorar. For the origin of the music sense there exist various theories: * a fusion of choro (from chorar) and Latin chorus * a corruption of choromeleiros, musicians during the Brazilian colonial period * a corruption of xolo, a type of dance from Brazilian fazendas.

phr: cry all the way to the bank

ety.text: From Middle English crystal, cristal, criȝstall, representing a merger of Old English cristalla (from Latin crystallus) and Anglo-Norman cristall, Old French cristal (from Latin crystallum). The Latin is derived from Ancient Greek κρύσταλλος (krústallos, “clear ice”), from κρύος (krúos, “frost”), from Proto-Indo-European *krews- (“hard, hard outer surface, crust”).

senses.d: A solid composed of an array of atoms or molecules possessing long-range order and arranged in a pattern which is periodic in three dimensions.
A piece of glimmering, shining mineral resembling ice or glass.
A fine type of glassware, or the material used to make it.
Crystal meth; methamphetamine hydrochloride.
A person's eye.
The glass over the dial of a watch case.
Made of crystal.
ex: The walls were crystal, and they seemed to have hundreds of different-colored lights shifting behind them.

senses.d: Very clear; coherent.
ex: "Do I make myself clear?" / "Crystal."

[…] the more faire and chriſtall is the skie,
The vglier ſeeme the cloudes that in it flye: […]

ety.text: Learned borrowing from Latin crystallum.
Borrowed from Latin crystallum, from Ancient Greek κρύσταλλος (krústallos).
Inherited from Old Spanish cristal, from Latin crystallum, from Ancient Greek κρύσταλλος (krústallos, “ice”).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cristal, crestal, from Latin crystallum (“crystal, ice”), from Ancient Greek κρύσταλλος (krústallos, “clear ice”), from κρύος (krúos, “frost”), from Proto-Indo-European *krus-, *kru- (“hard, hard outer surface, crust”).
From cry + -ing.

senses.d: That cries.
ex: The crying child on the street was evidently lost.

senses.d: That demands action or attention; desperate.
ex: There is a crying need for more manual workers in this country.

senses.d: That deserves rebuke or censure; deplorable.
ex: It is a crying shame that he managed to get away with that!

senses.d: The act of one who cries; a weeping or shouting.
ex: Their constant cryings kept us awake!
[…] their breathings, cryings, and excretings would have been damaged […]
